passages.t: Pray for everyone; one God and one mediator
passages.happening:
“First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone— for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity” (verses 1-2).

“This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all” (verses 3-6). Paul adds that this is why he was appointed ‘a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
‘First of all’ means first in importance. Before Paul says anything about how the church should be ordered, he says: pray. And pray ‘for everyone’.

Then he names the hardest people to pray for: ‘kings and all those in authority’. If Paul wrote this in the early 60s, the emperor was Nero. Christians were a small and often suspected group. Paul does not tell them to pray only for rulers they like. He tells them to pray for whoever rules. The goal is modest: ‘tranquil and quiet lives’, room to live godly lives in peace.

Why pray for everyone? Because of who God is. He ‘wants everyone to be saved’. The false teachers in Ephesus may have thought salvation was for a special few who had their secret knowledge. Paul says God's heart is as wide as the world.

Then comes what sounds like a short creed, perhaps one the church already said. ‘There is one God.’ That is Israel's great confession. ‘And there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.’ A mediator is a go-between who brings two sides together. Jesus can stand between God and humanity because he is both. Paul stresses ‘the man Christ Jesus’: the one who brings us to God shares our nature fully.

He ‘gave Himself as a ransom for all’. A ransom was a price paid to set someone free. The word Paul uses here appears only once in the New Testament; it is a stronger form of the word Jesus used when he said he came ‘to give His life as a ransom for many’ (Mark 10:45). It means a price paid in place of others.
passages.ot:
Praying for rulers, even foreign ones, was already the way of God's people. Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7). The Persian king ordered sacrifices in Jerusalem so that the people would “pray for the lives of the king and his sons” (Ezra 6:10). And Proverbs reminds us who is really in charge: “The king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1).

‘One God’ is the confession of Israel: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). And God's wide heart is already in the prophets: “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22). “For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live!” (Ezekiel 18:32).

Job longed for a go-between: “Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both” (Job 9:33). And Isaiah's servant “bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).
passages.hard:
Does praying for rulers mean supporting a particular ruler or party? And what does ‘one mediator’ mean?

Paul asks the church to pray for ‘kings and all those in authority’, whoever they are, and he was most likely writing under Nero. Prayer for rulers is not a vote for them, and it is not loyalty to a side. Believers on every side of a country's politics are asked to pray for those who govern, including those they did not choose and those they oppose. Nothing in these verses teaches a lesson for any party. The site's guide ‘Does the Kingdom of God Belong to a Political Party?’ says more.

‘One mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus’ is stated here as the church's confession. There is one God, and one go-between: Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, who gave himself as a ransom for all. Every Christian tradition confesses this.

And ‘who wants everyone to be saved’ has been read in different ways. Many read it as God's sincere desire for every person's salvation. Others, especially in the Reformed tradition, read ‘everyone’ as all kinds of people, rulers and ordinary people, Jews and Gentiles. A few have read it as a promise that every person will be saved in the end, though most Christians across the traditions reject that reading. These notes do not choose. On every reading, the church is to pray for everyone, and the gospel is for anyone.
passages.asks: Paul asks the church to pray first of all, and for everyone, including those in power. Ask whom you are leaving out of your prayers, and why. Ask whether you pray for leaders you did not vote for, and how you pray for them. And ask whether you know Jesus as the one mediator, the one who brings you to God.

passages.t: Men who pray without anger; women adorned with good deeds
passages.happening:
“Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension” (verse 8).

“Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Paul speaks first to the men. In the ancient world people often prayed standing with their hands raised, Jews, Greeks and Christians alike. Paul's concern is not the posture. It is the hands and the heart: ‘holy hands’, and prayer ‘without anger or dissension’. In a church split by false teaching and arguments over words, the men were apparently bringing their quarrels to prayer. Paul says you cannot lift angry hands to God.

Then he speaks to the women. Writers of the time, both pagan and Jewish, criticized women who wore elaborate hairstyles woven with gold and pearls and costly clothes. Such display showed off wealth, and could carry other messages too. In a church with rich and poor women sitting side by side, a rich woman flaunting her jewels in worship would shame the poor.

So Paul points them to a different kind of beauty: ‘good deeds’. The word ‘adorn’ is a word for arranging something beautifully. Paul says the most beautiful thing a woman who worships God can wear is a life of doing good. That is true of everyone.

Notice that both commands are about the same thing: how people come before God together. Men are not to come angry. Women are not to come showing off. Both are to come to God, not to each other.
passages.ot:
Lifting hands in prayer is old: “May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering” (Psalm 141:2). And clean hands mean a clean life: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” may stand in God's holy place (Psalm 24:3-4).

The prophets warned against proud display. Isaiah spoke of the daughters of Zion “jingling the bracelets on their ankles” (Isaiah 3:16), and said the Lord would take away their finery. Proverbs gives a better beauty: “Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (Proverbs 31:30). And God sees past the outside: “man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.asks: Paul asks men not to bring anger to prayer, and women not to bring display. Ask what you carry into worship that does not belong there: a grudge, a quarrel, a wish to be noticed. Ask what the people around you would see if they looked at your good deeds rather than your appearance. And ask whether there is anyone in your church whom your choices quietly shame.

passages.t: A woman must learn; ‘I do not permit a woman to teach’
passages.happening:
“A woman must learn in quietness and full submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet” (verses 11-12).

“For Adam was formed first, and then Eve. And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Start with the first command, which is easy to miss. ‘A woman must learn.’ In Paul's world many, Jews and Greeks alike, did not think women needed to be taught religious teaching. Paul assumes they will be taught. ‘Quietness and full submissiveness’ describes how any student was expected to learn from a teacher then: listening, not interrupting.

Then comes the hard verse: ‘I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.’ The word for ‘exercise authority’ appears only here in the whole New Testament, and only rarely in Greek before it. That is one reason these verses are read so differently.

Paul gives a reason from the beginning of Genesis: Adam was formed first, then Eve; and it was the woman who was deceived. How these reasons work is at the heart of the debate.

Notice the setting, which everyone agrees matters. This whole letter is about false teaching in Ephesus. The false teachers forbade marriage (4:3). Some younger widows were going from house to house saying things they should not (5:13), and some had ‘already turned aside to follow Satan’ (5:15). In his next letter Paul speaks of false teachers who ‘captivate vulnerable women’ (2 Timothy 3:6). How far that setting explains these verses is where Christians divide.

Notice too the family of words for ‘quiet’. It is the same family Paul used in verse 2 for the ‘quiet lives’ all believers should seek. It means a settled, peaceable manner more than total silence.

Two more points bear on both readings. For much of the church's history verse 14 was taken to mean that women are more easily deceived than men. Most complementarians and egalitarians today reject that reading. And the Greek words for ‘man’ and ‘woman’ also mean ‘husband’ and ‘wife’, so some read these verses as being about wives and husbands.
passages.ot:
Paul draws on Genesis 2 and 3. “Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground” (Genesis 2:7), and afterward God made the woman: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper” (Genesis 2:18). When God asked the woman what she had done, she said, “The serpent deceived me” (Genesis 3:13).

And the Old Testament also tells of women who spoke God's word to his people: “Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time” (Judges 4:4); and Huldah, whom the king's officials went to consult (2 Kings 22:14). How those women bear on this passage is read differently too.
passages.hard:
These verses are among the most disputed in the New Testament. What do Christians agree on, and where do they differ?

Christians who share the same faith in Christ read these verses differently. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith. These notes do not choose.

Much is agreed. Men and women are equally made in God's image, equally sinners, and equally saved by grace through faith in Christ. Paul tells women to learn, when many in his world did not. Women in the Bible prophesied, led and taught in many ways, and the church has always been carried by the faith and work of women. And nothing in this passage gives anyone leave to belittle, silence, frighten or control a woman, or to treat her as less than a sister in Christ.

Complementarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth before God, and that God has given them different callings in the church and the home, with the office of pastor or elder, and teaching the gathered church with that authority, given to qualified men. They read ‘to teach or to exercise authority over a man’ as two normal tasks of an elder, not two abuses, since the Greek pairs two actions of the same kind. They note that Paul's reason is not a local custom but the order of creation, ‘For Adam was formed first, and then Eve’, as he appeals to creation elsewhere (1 Corinthians 11:8-9), so they believe the rule is meant for every age. They agree that the Ephesus setting matters, but hold that Paul's reason reaches beyond it, and they note that the next chapter gives the work of teaching oversight to qualified men. And they gladly honour women teaching the faith in homes, groups, one to one, and in many other ways.

Egalitarian Christians believe that men and women are equal in worth and that every role in the church, including pastor and teacher, is open to both, as God gifts them. They read the rare word for ‘exercise authority’, used only here in the New Testament, as closer to ‘domineer’ or ‘seize authority’ than simply ‘lead’. They read the passage in its Ephesus setting: a church troubled from end to end by false teaching that had drawn in some women (5:13-15; 2 Timothy 3:6-7), with teachers who forbade marriage (4:3). On this reading the mention of Eve's deception is a picture of what was happening in Ephesus as women were misled by the false teachers, and Paul's present-tense ‘I do not permit’ describes his practice in that situation. They point to women elsewhere in the New Testament who prophesied (1 Corinthians 11:5), to Priscilla, who explained the way of God to Apollos (Acts 18:26), to Phoebe, ‘a servant of the church’, using the Greek word for deacon (Romans 16:1), and to Junia, whom the BSB calls ‘outstanding among the apostles’ (Romans 16:7).

The site's chapter note on 1 Timothy 2 sets out both readings more fully, and the note on Acts 18:24-28, where Priscilla and her husband teach Apollos, shows how each side reads that scene.
passages.asks: These verses divide faithful Christians, and both sides take them seriously. Ask whether you can state the view you do not hold in words its holders would sign. Ask whether the women in your church are being taught, honoured and heard. And whatever your view, ask whether your church is a place where no woman is belittled, silenced or controlled.

passages.happening:
Paul ends what he says about women with a promise and a condition: “Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control” (verse 15).

It is one of the hardest single verses in Paul's letters to read.
passages.hearers:
The Greek is harder than the English. It begins with ‘she will be saved’, as if still speaking of Eve, and then moves to ‘if they continue’. And it says ‘through the childbearing’, with ‘the’, using a word found nowhere else in the New Testament.

Remember the setting. The false teachers in Ephesus forbade marriage (4:3). Some may have taught that a truly spiritual woman would turn her back on marriage and children. Paul has just spoken of Eve's deception. Now he turns at once to hope: the story of the woman does not end in the fall.

Notice the condition, which is the same for every believer: to ‘continue in faith, love, and holiness’. Paul has already said, earlier in this very chapter, that God ‘wants everyone to be saved’ through the one mediator, Christ Jesus (2:4-5). Whatever verse 15 means, it does not set up a second way of being saved for women.

The word ‘saved’ in Paul can mean final salvation, or being kept safe, or living out salvation day by day. Which sense he means here is part of the puzzle.
passages.ot:
Genesis 3 holds the first promise of a child who would defeat evil, spoken to the serpent: “And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel” (Genesis 3:15). Some readers hear that promise behind ‘the childbearing’.

The next verse speaks of the pain of childbirth: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth” (Genesis 3:16). Others hear that behind Paul's words.

And the Old Testament knows the grief of women who longed for children, and God's care for them: Hannah prayed, and later said, “I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him” (1 Samuel 1:27). And Isaiah promised faithful eunuchs, who could have no children, “a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5).
passages.hard:
Verse 15, ‘saved through childbearing’, is a puzzle of its own. Some read it as the birth of the Saviour, the child promised to the woman in Genesis 3:15, since the Greek says ‘the childbearing’. Some read it as a promise that women would be kept safe through childbirth. Some read it as women living out their salvation in ordinary family life, against false teachers who forbade marriage. All agree on the condition Paul gives: that they ‘continue in faith, love, and holiness’.

On every reading, it does not mean that a woman is saved by having children. Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, for women and men alike. No woman's salvation or worth depends on bearing children. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.
passages.asks: Paul says the way of salvation for every believer is to continue in faith, love and holiness. Ask whether you are continuing in those today. Ask whether anyone in your church has been made to feel less because they have no children, and what you could do about it. And if this verse has hurt you, hear it again: no one's salvation or worth depends on bearing children.
